F OR the administration of President Bola Tinubu, the National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention is an emergency response aligned with its Renewed Hope Agenda. To millions of Nigerians, however, it is another government handout that raises more questions than answers, particularly as the country inches towards the 2027 general elections. The timing alone invites suspicion. On the face of it, the intervention is commendable. Cash transfers are a legitimate social protection tool used by governments across the world to cushion the effects of economic hardship on the poorest households. But the programme is a damning admission of the depth of poverty under the Tinubu administration. A government that must periodically dole out N50,000 to keep millions of its citizens afloat is presiding over an economy that has failed to provide basic economic security for its people. The scale of the crisis is frightening. The Nigeria Living Standards Survey estimated that 139 million Nigerians lived below the poverty line in 2025, up from 82.9 million, or 40.1 per cent of the population, in 2018/19. By 2022/23, the figure had risen to 113 million, representing 56 per cent of the population. PricewaterhouseCoopers paints an equally grim picture. Its Nigeria Economic Outlook 2026 projects that at least 141 million Nigerians, or 62 per cent of the population, will be poorer by December 2026. According to the firm, the policy adjustments introduced to stabilise the economy have yet to translate into tangible improvements in citizens’ living conditions. The United Nations has also projected that about 64 per cent of Nigerians could face hunger by 2030. These figures expose the human cost of the government’s economic reforms. The removal of the fuel subsidy, currency devaluation and other policy adjustments have triggered severe inflation and made the cost of food, transportation, housing and essential services beyond the reach of millions. Rather than provide meaningful relief, the government has repeatedly urged Nigerians to endure the pain in anticipation of better days. Now, it has suddenly discovered the virtues of cash handouts. Ostensibly, the N50,000 intervention is intended to cushion the impact of rising food inflation and the prohibitive cost of essential goods. But how much relief can N50,000 possibly provide in an economy where the purchasing power of the naira has been so severely eroded? It may offer temporary respite to a struggling household, but it will hardly make a dent in the poverty that government policies and economic failures have helped to deepen. Coordinated by the National Social Safety-Nets Coordinating Office, the programme involves digital payments to vulnerable Nigerians through licensed financial service providers, including ALAT by Wema, MoMo PSB, NairaGram, Opay and Moniepoint. There are no sufficiently clear and publicly accessible baseline metrics for determining vulnerability across the country’s diverse regions. Nor is there adequate information about the geographical spread, selection process and actual number of intended beneficiaries. Even the duration of the programme is muddled. While the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Bernard Doro, announced it as a monthly stipend, other official documentation describes it as a one-off payment. This is no minor administrative discrepancy. Nigerians deserve to know whether the government is offering a single N50,000 payment or a recurring intervention, and for how long. A social protection programme cannot be run on contradictory official pronouncements. The selection process is equally troubling. Rather than provide an open and transparent application process, beneficiaries are reportedly drawn from verified national identity records and the National Social Register, said to contain more than 70 million poor and vulnerable Nigerians. But the government has not adequately explained the criteria used to determine eligibility, how the records are verified or how excluded but deserving households can challenge their omission. There is already sufficient reason to be wary. The Auditor-General of the Federation’s 2024 Annual Report, published on August 7, 2026, raised serious questions about expenditure by key humanitarian agencies between 2023 and 2024. SERAP demands release of detained FIJ journalist Ojukwu When gold has two masters: Demand versus rates and inflation The naira, the poor and the powerful Among other things, it questioned N33.751 billion reportedly transferred to more than 3.2 million households across 35 states in 2023, citing inadequate documentation to verify payments and reconcile beneficiary records. The report identified alleged irregularities involving N36.74 billion in payments without prepayment audits, N4.61 billion in unsupported expenditure, N350.18 million for enrolment, N89.51 million for store purchases and N17.42 million in diesel advances. These are not trivial accounting discrepancies. They concern public funds ostensibly earmarked for some of the country’s poorest citizens. The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project has since approached the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, challenging alleged financial irregularities involving more than N78.8 billion in federal cash-transfer and social protection funds. The suit, which draws on the Auditor-General’s findings, names the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, the National Cash Transfer Office and the National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office. SERAP is asking the court to declare that the alleged failure to account for funds allocated to cash-transfer and social protection programmes violates Nigeria’s international human rights obligations. These are serious allegations that demand thorough investigation and accountability. It would be reckless for the government to launch another intervention without first addressing the credibility questions surrounding previous programmes. Against this background, it is difficult to dismiss the political undertones of the N50,000 relief package. Having repeatedly asked Nigerians to endure unprecedented hardship while promising that the reforms would eventually yield dividends, Tinubu’s administration is now offering cash relief as the 2027 elections approach. The government has a responsibility to demonstrate that this is a genuine social protection measure, not an elaborate attempt to cultivate electoral goodwill with public money. Beyond the politics and accounting questions, there is a more fundamental issue: what exactly is the government trying to achieve? The government must publish the number of beneficiaries, the states and communities covered, the eligibility criteria, the payment schedule and the mechanisms for independent verification. It must provide an accessible complaints and redress system to address exclusion, fraud and payment failures. Above all, the programme must be subjected to independent audits, with the findings made public. The intervention must not become another vehicle for political patronage or a disguised campaign instrument for the ruling party ahead of 2027. Public resources are not campaign funds, and poverty must never be exploited as an electoral weapon. More importantly, the government must stop treating handouts as an economic strategy. Nigeria needs massive investment in infrastructure, particularly roads, railways and reliable electricity, to reduce production costs, stimulate economic activity and create jobs. It must pursue policies that tame inflation, expand agricultural production, strengthen food supply chains and make essential commodities affordable. Functional healthcare and education systems are equally indispensable. Small and Medium Enterprises must be given a conducive operating environment, access to affordable financing and reliable infrastructure to expand, employ more people and generate wealth. These are the foundations of sustainable poverty reduction, not periodic cash transfers. There is nothing inherently wrong with giving N50,000 to a struggling Nigerian. The problem is when a government mistakes temporary relief for meaningful economic intervention, or worse, uses public money to purchase political goodwill while leaving the conditions that produce poverty untouched. Nigerians do not need a government that periodically distributes crumbs from an economy in distress. They need one that creates the conditions for them to earn decent incomes, feed their families and live with dignity. The ultimate measure of social protection is not how much money government hands out, but how many people it lifts out of poverty permanently. Punch Editorial Board
